{{Short description|Sequence of end-to-end vectors across points of a lattice}}
[[File:Lattice Path in Z2.svg|thumb|285px|Lattice path of length 5 in {{bug workaround|{{math|ℤ{{sup|2}}}}}} with {{math|1=''S'' = { (2,0), (1,1), (0,-1) }.}}|right]]

In [[combinatorics]], a '''lattice path''' {{mvar|L}} in the {{mvar|d}}-dimensional [[integer lattice]] {{tmath|\mathbb{Z}^d}} of length {{mvar|k}} with steps in the [[Set (mathematics)|set]] {{mvar|S}}, is a sequence of [[Vector (mathematics and physics)|vector]]s {{tmath|v_0, v_1, \ldots, v_k \in \mathbb{Z}^d}} such that each consecutive difference <math>v_i - v_{i-1}</math> lies in {{mvar|S}}.<ref name=EC1>{{cite book|authorlink=Richard P. Stanley|last=Stanley|first=Richard|title=Enumerative Combinatorics, Volume 1|date=2012|publisher=Cambridge University Press|isbn=978-1-107-60262-5|pages=21|edition=2}}</ref> 
A lattice path may lie in any [[Lattice (group)|lattice]] in {{tmath|\mathbb{R}^d}},<ref name=EC1 /> but the integer lattice {{tmath|\mathbb{Z}^d}} is most commonly used.

An example of a lattice path in {{tmath|\mathbb{Z}^2}} of length 5 with steps in <math> S = \lbrace (2,0), (1,1), (0,-1) \rbrace </math>
is <math> L = \lbrace (-1,-2), (0,-1), (2,-1), (2,-2), (2,-3), (4,-3) \rbrace </math>.

==North-East lattice paths==
A '''North-East (NE) lattice path''' is a lattice path in <math> \mathbb{Z}^2 </math> with steps in <math> S = \lbrace (0,1), (1,0) \rbrace </math>. The <math> (0,1) </math> steps are called North steps and denoted by <math> N </math>s; the <math> (1,0) </math> steps are called East steps and denoted by <math> E </math>s.

NE lattice paths most commonly begin at the origin. This convention allows encoding all the information about a NE lattice path <math> L </math> in a single [[permutation pattern|permutation word]]. The length of the word gives the number of steps of the lattice path, <math> k </math>. The order of the <math> N </math>s and <math> E </math>s communicates the sequence of <math> L </math>. Furthermore, the number of <math> N </math>s and the number of <math> E </math>s in the word determines the end point of <math> L </math>.

If the permutation word for a NE lattice path contains <math> n </math> <math> N </math>-steps and <math> e </math> <math> E </math>-steps, and if the path begins at the origin, then the path necessarily ends at <math> (e,n) </math>. This follows because the path "walks" exactly <math> n </math> steps North and <math> e </math> steps East from <math> (0,0) </math>.

[[File:1N3E SVG.svg|thumb|500px|The four NE lattice paths starting from <math>(0,0)</math> with exactly one <math>N</math> and three <math>E</math>s. The endpoint is necessarily at <math>(3,1)</math>.|center]]

==Counting lattice paths==
Lattice paths are often used to count other combinatorial objects. Similarly, there are many combinatorial objects that count the number of lattice paths of a certain kind. This occurs when the lattice paths are in [[bijection]] with the object in question. For example,

* [[Catalan number#Applications in combinatorics|Dyck paths]] are counted by the <math> n^{\text{th}} </math> [[Catalan number]] <math> C_n </math>. A '''Dyck path''' is a lattice path in <math>\mathbb{Z}^2</math> from <math> (0,0) </math> to <math> (2n,0) </math> with steps in <math> S = \lbrace (1,1), (1,-1) \rbrace </math> that never passes below the <math>x</math>-axis.<ref name=EC2>{{cite book|authorlink=Richard P. Stanley|last=Stanley|first=Richard|title=Enumerative Combinatorics, Volume 2|date=2001|publisher=Cambridge University Press|isbn=978-0-521-78987-5|pages=173, 239}}</ref> Equivalently, a Dyck path is a NE lattice path from <math> (0,0) </math> to <math> (n,n) </math> that lies strictly below (but may touch) the diagonal <math> y=x </math>.<ref name=EC2 /><ref name=Wolfram_Dyck>{{cite web|title=Wolfram MathWorld|url=http://mathworld.wolfram.com/DyckPath.html|accessdate=6 March 2014}}</ref>
* The [[Schröder number]]s count the number of lattice paths from <math> (0,0) </math> to <math> (n,n) </math> with steps in <math> (1,0), (0,1) </math> and <math> (1,1) </math> that never rise above the diagonal <math> y=x </math>.<ref name=EC2 />
* The number of NE lattice paths from <math> (0,0) </math> to <math> (a,b) </math> counts the number of [[combination]]s of <math> a </math> objects out of a set of <math> a + b </math> objects.

==Combinations and NE lattice paths==
NE lattice paths have close connections to the number of [[combination]]s, which are counted by the [[binomial coefficient]], and arranged in [[Pascal's triangle]]. The diagram below demonstrates some of these connections.

[[File:Walking on Pascal's Triangle SVG.svg|thumb|300px|The number of lattice paths from <math> (0,0) </math> to <math> (2,3) </math> is equal to <math> \binom{2+3}{2} =\binom{5}{2} = 10 </math>.|center]]

The number of lattice paths from <math> (0,0) </math> to <math> (n,k) </math> is equal to the [[binomial coefficient]] <math> \binom{n+k}{n} </math>. The diagram shows this for <math> 0 \leq k \leq n =4 </math>. If one rotates the diagram 135° clockwise about the origin and extends it to include all <math> n,k \in \mathbb{N} \cup \lbrace 0 \rbrace </math>, then one obtains Pascal's triangle. This result is because the <math> k^{\text{th}} </math> entry of the <math> n^{\text{th}} </math> row of Pascal's Triangle is the binomial coefficient <math> \binom{n}{k} </math>.

===Problems and proofs===
The graphical representation of NE lattice paths lends itself to many [[bijective]] proofs involving combinations. Here are a few examples.

* <math> \sum_{k=0}^n \binom{n}{k} ^2 = \binom{2n}{n}. </math>

''Proof'': The right-hand side is equal to the number of NE lattice paths from <math> (0,0) </math> to <math> (n,n) </math>. Each of these NE lattice paths intersects exactly one of the lattice points in the rectangular array with coordinates <math> (x, n-x) </math> for <math> x \in \lbrace 0, 1, \ldots, n \rbrace </math>. This is shown in the figure below for <math> n=4 </math>: Every NE lattice path from <math> (0,0) </math> to <math> (4,4) </math> intersects exactly one of the colored nodes.

[[Image:NE nodes SVG.svg|thumb|Each NE lattice path passes through exactly one colored node.|center]]

On the left-hand side, the [[binomial coefficient]] squared, <math> \binom{n}{k}^2</math>, represents two copies of the set of NE lattice paths from <math> (0,0) </math> to <math> (k,n-k) </math> attached endpoint-to-startpoint. Rotating the second copy 90° clockwise does not change the combinatorics of the object: <math> \binom{n}{k} = \binom{n}{n-k} </math>. So the total number of lattice paths remains the same.

[[Image:Squared.png|thumb|500px|Sets of NE lattice paths squared, with the second copy rotated 90° clockwise.|center]]

Superimpose the NE lattice paths squared onto the same rectangular array, as seen in the figure below. We see that all NE lattice paths from <math> (0,0) </math> to <math> (n,n) </math> are accounted for. In particular, any lattice path passing through the red lattice point (for example) is counted by the squared set of lattice paths (also shown in red). <math> \Box </math>

[[File:Superimposed lattice paths squared.jpg|thumb|200px|Superimposed sets of NE lattice paths squared. All NE lattice paths are accounted for.|center]]
